paras: The threatened lynching of Nathan M. Reed took place at Alexandria City, Alabama, in August 1888, when a lynching party was organized against Reed, a farmer about sixty years old who had been jailed on an accusation of killing his wife. The Alexandria City Rifles were called out to guard the jail, and the reports credited the militia alone with saving his life.

According to a special from Alexandria City, Reed lived three miles from town, was a member of the Baptist church and an officer in several secret societies, and had grown children. The dispatch said he had recently been "paying attention" to his wife's sister, a woman of about twenty-five.

On the morning before the dispatch, Reed's wife reportedly accused him of intimacy with her sister, and he was said to have seized her by the throat and choked her to the floor. Mrs. Reed, described as in delicate health, died that night, and Reed was arrested and put in jail.

News of the death spread quickly and caused "intense excitement," and a lynching party was organized. That evening, probably August 18, the Alexandria City Rifles were called out to guard the jail, and "only the presence of the military at the jail saved Reed's life."
No report of an attack on the jail, an inquest, or a trial of Reed appears in the coverage.

The story reached northern and southern papers as a short Birmingham wire item that gave no race for Reed or for the lynching party. The Wilmington Evening Journal ran it on August 20 under "Soldiers Prevent a Lynching," and the Midland Journal of Rising Sun, Maryland, printed a shortened version on August 24 headed "Saved by the Militia." The Atlanta Constitution carried the fullest text on August 28, dated August 19, under "Theratened With Lynching."

Each version opened by calling Reed "accused of wife murder" but went on to describe the killing as "his crime" and to dwell on his standing and the alleged affair. The versions differed slightly: the Wilmington text said Reed had been married thirty years, the Atlanta text thirty-five.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Nathan M. Reed
bases: A lynching party was organized against Reed, a jailed man accused of killing his wife, and the militia guarded the jail; no killing was reported (A1, A3).
Reed was not killed: the papers say only the presence of the military at the jail saved his life, so this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one (A1, A3).
Both full reports (A1, A3) and the reprint (A2) repeat one special from Alexandria City sent through Birmingham in nearly identical words, so there is one underlying account.

accounts.label: Birmingham wire from an Alexandria City special
accounts.gist: The Alexandria City Rifles were called out to prevent the lynching of Reed, accused of choking his wife to death after she accused him of intimacy with her sister; only the military saved him.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Soldiers Prevent a Lynching' and 'Theratened With Lynching'; the item stresses Reed's standing and the alleged infidelity and calls the killing 'his crime'.
A Maryland weekly ran a shortened version headed 'Saved by the Militia'.

conflicts.note: Minor discrepancy between versions of the same wire; the Atlanta Constitution text is the fuller one.
The Wilmington paper may have dated the wire by its own publication day; the Aug. 19 dateline with 'last evening' puts the call-out on about Aug. 18.

info: Militia called out on the evening of about Aug. 18, 1888 ('last evening' in a dispatch dated Aug. 19); the wife was choked 'yesterday morning' and died 'last night'

Nathan M. Reed, a farmer about sixty years old, threatened with lynching; race not stated
